message:
MESSAGE:
I'm redoing our downstairs bathroom floor myself (first time, slightly terrified) and I've got a pile of questions.

The tile shop guy talked really fast so I didn't catch half of it. Could you explain what "lippage" means in tiling, in simple terms? And what's a sensible grout colour for a pale grey porcelain tile if I don't want it looking dirty after a month? My partner also wants to know whether we should do the floor before or after the new toilet goes in, just a quick answer with a reason.

The floor is 2.4 m by 1.8 m. The tiles I like are 30 cm × 60 cm and come in boxes of 8. Everyone online says to add 10% for cuts and breakages. How many boxes do I actually need to buy?

I also need a short, polite message to the neighbours saying there'll be some noise from cutting tiles on Saturday morning, since they've already put up with a skip on the drive for a fortnight. Finally, any three tips for a beginner laying their first floor would be very welcome. I've watched a lot of videos, but they all make it look far easier than it probably is.

Thank you, honestly.

REQUESTS:
1. Explain what 'lippage' means in tiling
2. Suggest a grout colour for pale grey porcelain tile
3. Say whether to tile before or after fitting the new toilet, with a reason
4. Calculate how many boxes of 30x60 cm tiles (8 per box) are needed for a 2.4 x 1.8 m floor plus 10% waste  KEY: Area = 2.4 x 1.8 = 4.32 m^2; tile = 0.3 x 0.6 = 0.18 m^2, so 24 tiles exactly. Plus 10% = 26.4, round up to 27 tiles. 27/8 = 3.375, so 4 boxes (32 tiles). 3 boxes (24 tiles) is the no-waste shortcut and would leave them short. Answer: 4 boxes.
5. Write a short polite message to neighbours about tile-cutting noise
6. Give three tips for a beginner laying a floor

ANSWER:
## How many boxes: **4**

| Step | Calculation | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Floor area | 2.4 m × 1.8 m | 4.32 m² |
| Tile area | 0.3 m × 0.6 m | 0.18 m² |
| Tiles to cover the floor | 4.32 ÷ 0.18 | 24 |
| Plus 10% | 24 × 1.1 | 26.4, so 27 tiles |
| Boxes of 8 | 27 ÷ 8 | 3.4, round up to **4 boxes (32 tiles)** |

Three boxes would give exactly 24 tiles, with nothing spare for a single cut or breakage. Four boxes give 8 spare tiles, which is the right amount for a first job. Long tiles in a small room usually waste more than 10%, especially in a staggered pattern.

Check that all four boxes have the same batch or shade number, and keep a couple of spares afterwards for future repairs.

## What "lippage" means

**Lippage is when one tile's edge sits higher than the tile next to it**, so you get a little ridge you can feel with your foot or see when light falls across the floor. It's usually caused by an uneven floor, uneven adhesive, or slightly bowed tiles. Long tiles like yours are more prone to it.

The shop may have mentioned two common fixes:
- **Tile levelling clips**, cheap plastic clips that pull neighbouring edges flush;
- **Avoiding a half-tile stagger with 30 × 60 tiles.** Offset each row by a third of a tile instead, so slightly bowed tiles don't meet at their highest points.

## Grout colour

**Go for a mid grey, a shade or two darker than the tile.** It hides dirt much better than white or pale grey, and it still looks neat. A stain-resistant grout, or sealing a standard grout, will help it stay clean.

## Floor before or after the toilet?

**Tile first, then fit the toilet.** The toilet then sits on the finished floor and can be sealed properly. You also won't have awkward cuts around its base, or an untiled patch if you ever change toilets.

## Message to the neighbours

> Hi [names], just a heads-up that we'll be cutting tiles on Saturday morning from about [time], so there may be some noise for a few hours. Thanks so much for your patience with the work, and with the skip on the drive these last two weeks. We really appreciate it, and it should all be finished soon!

## Three tips for your first floor

1. **Prepare the floor before anything else.** It needs to be solid, clean and flat. Check it with a long straightedge, and level any dips first. A timber floor usually needs plywood or tile backer board on top. Most tiling problems, including lippage and cracked tiles, start with the floor underneath.
2. **Lay the tiles out dry before you mix any adhesive.** Plan from the centre of the room so you don't end up with thin slivers at the doorway or along one wall. Thin cuts are hard to make and look obvious.
3. **Work in small sections, with full adhesive coverage.** Mix small batches. With large tiles, spread adhesive on the back of each tile as well as the floor, and use levelling clips. Leave a small gap at the walls for expansion. Let the adhesive set fully, usually around 24 hours (check the bag), before grouting or walking on it.

The videos do make it look easy. Being careful with preparation and layout is what makes your first floor look professional.
